title: Contentment with decree

cards: A son named Ibrahim is dying, and his father is the Prophet ﷺ. The father's eyes fill with tears. A companion is surprised to see it, and asks, in effect, you too, Messenger of Allah?
His answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, holds two things at once. The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And then, to his son: we are saddened by your parting.
Tears, and grief, and no complaint against Allah, all in the same breath.

teach.b: The station is rida, being pleased, or content, with what Allah decrees. It sits right beside patience, and teachers of the path draw the difference carefully. Patience is holding steady when the taste is bitter.

teach.h: THE EYE WEEPS, THE HEART GRIEVES.
teach.b: Rida goes a step further: the taste is still bitter, but the heart has stopped arguing with the One who served it. That's why the Prophet's tears matter so much. Rida is not a smile pasted over grief.
He wept. He said he was saddened. What he didn't do was say anything against his Lord.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as a way of life, and with Muhammad as messenger has tasted the taste of faith. Notice the first thing on that list.
Not pleased with every event; pleased with Allah, as Lord.
And the Qur'an describes the pleasure going both ways, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah hath pleasure in them and they have pleasure in Him." Two more things rida is not.
It isn't approving of wrong. Scholars distinguish accepting what Allah has decreed from accepting an injustice someone is doing, which you're still asked to stop if you can.
And it isn't giving up effort; yesterday's camel still gets tied. You don't have to like the weather. You can stop shouting at the sky.
And if grief ever feels like too much to carry, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

how: Muslims describe rida as contentment with Allah's decree that still allows grief and tears, and some repeat the words 'I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as my way of life, and with Muhammad as messenger' in their morning and evening remembrance.

o: rida: contentment with Allah as Lord, even through tears
approving of every wrong, since all of it was decreed
never crying or grieving, whatever happens to you

s: the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son Ibrahim, and said his heart grieved.
in the Qur'an, the pleasure goes both ways
"Allah hath pleasure in them and they have pleasure in Him."
being content with decree means accepting injustice
scholars distinguish Allah's decree from a wrong someone is doing, which is still to be stopped if possible.

games.q: the Prophet ﷺ sits with his dying son Ibrahim, and his eyes fill with tears. a companion is surprised. what does the Prophet say?
o: I shouldn't be weeping. forgive me.
the eye weeps, the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
games.why: in Sahih al-Bukhari, he keeps the tears and the grief, and says nothing against his Lord. that's rida.

practice: Choose something small you've been quietly arguing with, the rain, a delay, a plan that changed; not an injustice, just a thing that is how it is.
Notice the but it should have been different, and for one breath set the argument down; you're allowed to wish it were otherwise.
If you pray, you can say radhitu billahi rabba, I am pleased with Allah as Lord; if not, simply say inside: this is how it is today.

wordCard.voice: Rida. Contentment: being pleased with Allah as Lord, so that even through tears the heart stops arguing with what He has decreed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pleased with him. Tears allowed, and no argument with the sky. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah hath pleasure in them and they have pleasure in Him.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 (the death of Ibrahim: the eye weeps, the heart grieves)
